summary: An April 1st joke RFC that proposes a TCP option to denote packet mood. It is humorous, not a real protocol, and is published for informational purposes.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes adding emoticons to TCP packets. It assigns moods to events such as retransmissions, while noting that packets do not actually feel.

questions: what is the tcp mood option
how does the packet mood option work
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposes emoticons for labeling TCP packet moods.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines a way to label feelings that people infer from packet behavior.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes a variable-length TCP option carrying two or three 7-bit ASCII characters, such as an emoticon.
tldr.outcome: It is humor, not an Internet Standards Track specification; the text says any IANA assignment would depend on standardization.

today: RFC 5841 is an Informational April 1st joke document. It makes no claim that the proposed option was standardized or deployed.

sections.title: The Packet Mood Idea
sections.content:
This April 1st RFC jokes about adding emotion labels to TCP packets. It says packets cannot feel, but suggests that people could infer a mood from events such as a missing acknowledgement or a retransmission.

The proposed labels are ASCII emoticons in a TCP option. The RFC frames them as a reflection of the user's mood, not a property packets possess.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is an April 1st joke. It proposes labels that describe how a person might interpret packet behavior.

sections.title: The Proposed Option
sections.content:
The proposal uses TCP option kind 25, with a variable length of four or five bytes. The option contains two or three 7-bit ASCII characters, sent in 8-bit bytes with the leading bit set to zero. Multiple mood options could appear in one TCP header.

The RFC lists emoticons such as :) for happy, :( for sad, and >:@ for angry. Its examples show the kind, length and ASCII characters.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries a short ASCII emoticon. The RFC gives examples for several proposed moods.

sections.title: When Packets Would Get a Mood
sections.content:
The RFC offers humorous rules for assigning moods. For example, it suggests happy labels after acknowledgements arrive quickly without retransmissions, angry labels for retransmitted packets, and confused labels for acknowledgements sent after out-of-order delivery.

Applications would define their own preconditions for several labels. The RFC also notes that TCP options use space that would otherwise be available for data, and warns that an attacker could alter a mood label.
sections.plainLanguage: The suggested labels depend on network events or message content. Adding the option also takes space from the packet's data.

references.text: Postel, J., "Transmission Control Protocol", STD 7, RFC 793, September 1981.
